name: David Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, David. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in by half seven at the Hollis Supply depot on the ring road, and the first thing I do is print the overnight stock report, because I like it on paper. Then it's phone calls about copper pipe, valves and boiler spares, chasing the reps about what's late. Afternoons I raise purchase orders on our old ordering system and argue with suppliers about copper prices, which move every week. I like the haggling and knowing the reps by name, but the late lorries wear me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you like it on paper. How do you get on with the newer tools at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Badly, honestly. Raj, the other buyer, uses some AI thing to write his supplier emails, and I just pick up the phone. I've never used one of those chatbots, not even on my phone. I'm at the lower end of pay for this job, and Lena and I rent a small flat above a launderette, so I don't take chances with anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. At work I'd tell Raj his chatbot turned out to be a fancy spellchecker. Online I'd probably share something about bosses wasting money on software while they froze our pay. That's my real point: the money went to the wrong place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's a relief, but it doesn't fix my actual problem. If nothing changes, I'm still a buyer on lower pay with about three weeks of rent saved. Hollis has frozen pay two years running, and the only other distributor is fifty kilometres away. So the boring future is still a tight one for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job the way I do it, phones and paper. I'd ask the union rep at the depot whether buyers can be part of the next pay claim, because right now it's only the warehouse staff. And I'd try to put fifty a month away so there's more than three weeks between me and trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved, a bit flat. Picturing it is like dodging a storm and then remembering the roof still leaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the pay freeze. What's the first thing that goes if money gets tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably, which sounds mad because I need it to get to the depot. But it's a twelve-year-old hatchback and the insurance is killing me. I'd sooner get the bus and add forty minutes than miss rent. Lena would go back to extra night shifts at the care home, and I hate that idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you think about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Raj a bit, because he's put real effort into the AI stuff and it'd come to nothing special. But mostly the warehouse team, because they never get a rise when margins are tight. Gavin, the commercial manager, always says margins are tight. Even in the boring world, someone has to push for a fair share.

say: I'd tell my colleague the **AI hype** turned out to be a fancy spellchecker.
I'd post that bosses **wasted money** on software while freezing our pay.
think: Privately it's a **relief**, but my real problem is lower pay and three weeks of rent saved.
With a **pay freeze** and the next distributor fifty kilometres away, the boring future is still tight.
do: Keep working by **phone and paper**, exactly as now.
Ask the depot **union rep** to include buyers in the next pay claim.
Save **fifty a month** to get past three weeks of rent.
feel: **Relieved** but flat, like dodging a storm and remembering the roof still leaks.
S0.quote: If nothing changes, I'm still a buyer on lower pay with about three weeks of rent saved.
fieldNote: His worry is **money**, not machines: the pay freeze and thin savings drive everything he says.
He sees the plateau as a **fairness** story about where the firm's money goes.
He'd give up the **car** before missing rent, which shows how close to the edge he lives.

steps.text: Keep phoning suppliers and printing the morning stock report
Ask the depot union rep to include buyers in the pay claim
Put fifty a month aside towards a bigger rent cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice bosses are making, not the weather. Online I'd be the one posting that if software does our ordering, the savings should go into wages, not to the owners. At work I'd say it out loud in the canteen, which wouldn't make me popular with Gavin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm the one who goes. Buying is exactly the list on that card: ordering, checking, chasing. If my boss has to choose between me and the other buyer, he keeps the one who already uses the tools. I'm not daft, I can see that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd get the union to push for buyers to be covered, with a rule that nobody's let go without paid retraining. I'd stop the gym and the streaming and save every bit I can, maybe a hundred a month. And I'd quietly ask about the warehouse supervisor job, because forklifts and loading bays don't care about chatbots yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Angry too, because I'd be blamed for being slow when the real story is a firm saving money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've never used these tools. Would you try them, if it meant keeping the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try, if someone sat with me and showed me, and the firm paid for the time. I won't do it on my own evenings for free so they can let me go faster. Lena says I'm being stubborn, and she's probably half right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena the night you heard about the cuts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we can't renew the lease if the rent goes up again. We'd probably have to move in with her mum for a bit, which neither of us wants. Lena would say we'll manage, she always does. I'd lie awake doing sums anyway.

say: I'd say cutting buyers is a **choice bosses make**, not the weather.
I'd post that any **savings** from software should go into wages, not to the owners.
think: My job is **ordering, checking and chasing**, exactly what the card says AI takes.
If one buyer goes, it's **me**, because the other buyer already uses the tools.
do: Push the **union** for a rule that nobody goes without paid retraining.
Cut the gym and streaming to save about **a hundred** a month.
Ask quietly about the **warehouse supervisor** job on the depot floor.
feel: A bit **sick** about losing the job.
**Angry** that he'd be called slow when the firm is just saving money.
S1.quote: If my boss has to choose between me and the other buyer, he keeps the one who already uses the tools.
fieldNote: He's clear-eyed that he'd be **first out**, and that clarity sits next to real anger.
He'd learn AI only on **paid time**; on his own evenings it feels like training his replacement.
The **lease** and a move to his partner's mother are the concrete fear underneath.

steps.text: Push the union to cover buyers with paid retraining before cuts
Cancel the gym and streaming to save a hundred a month
Ask about the warehouse supervisor job at the Hollis depot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to step in, full stop. If thinking work goes in two years, you need wage support and a real plan, not a website telling people to learn to code. I'd be at every union meeting and probably on the march.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't think I'd have a job by 2028. Buying is all screen and phone, there's nothing hands-on about it. The warehouse staff get three more years before the robots, but I don't even get that. I've got three weeks of rent and no idea what I'd be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd go to the warehouse manager and ask for any floor job, loading or picking, because hands-on work buys three years. I'd sign up for my forklift licence, which is a few hundred, and borrow it from my dad if I had to. When the buying job goes, I'd claim whatever support exists and we'd move into Lena's mum's spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. I don't have a plan, and two years isn't long enough to save my way to one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots come three years later. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The warehouse is the lifeboat, and it's a small one. There are maybe twenty jobs on that floor and half the office would want them. And in 2031 the robots come for those too. So it's not a plan, it's a waiting room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've talked about the union a lot. What would you actually want them to win?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay that carries on for a year after you're let go, and the firm paying for real training, like a trade. And some say in how fast it happens. I know a union at a small distributor can't stop AGI. But I'd rather be in a room fighting than sitting at home refreshing job sites.

say: I'd say the **government** must step in with wage support and a real plan.
I'd be at every **union meeting** and probably on the march.
think: My job is all **screen and phone**, so I'd have nothing left by 2028.
With three weeks of rent saved, I have **no idea** what I'd become.
do: Ask the warehouse manager for any **floor job**, loading or picking.
Get a **forklift licence**, borrowing the few hundred from his dad.
Claim **support** and move into his partner's mother's spare room.
feel: Like the **floor's gone**, with no plan and no time to save for one.
S2.quote: The warehouse is the lifeboat, and it's a small one. There are maybe twenty jobs on that floor and half the office would want them.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year robot gap** helping warehouse staff, not him, since his work is all screen.
His only move is to **step down** onto the depot floor, which he calls a waiting room.
Under the union talk he's **frozen**: no savings, no plan, no time.

steps.text: Ask the warehouse manager for a loading or picking job
Get a forklift licence with money borrowed from his dad
Push the union for a year of pay after any layoff
Move into his partner's mother's spare room if the job goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but louder, because now there's no excuse. Five years is enough time for the government and firms to plan properly. I'd say if they waste it, that's on them, not on people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better, I won't pretend it isn't. I'd be thirty-two when it lands, young enough to learn a trade. But I'd be starting at the bottom on apprentice money with no savings. And the robots arrive in 2034, so any hands-on trade only buys me a few years more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at plumbing, because I already know every part in the catalogue. The college in town runs evening courses for about eight hundred a year. I'd keep the buying job while I study and save what's left, and keep pushing the union for paid training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but less frozen. There's a gap I could squeeze through, if I'm lucky with money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You know every part in the catalogue. Does that count for anything in a trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I know what a compression fitting is and why the cheap valves fail. Plumbers ring me to ask about parts all the time, but knowing the parts isn't the same as fitting them under someone's sink. I'd be older and slower than the eighteen-year-olds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you won't learn AI on your own time. Would you study plumbing on your own time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I would, and I see the contradiction. A plumbing ticket is mine to keep, wherever I go. An AI course is me training my own replacement for the firm. That's how it feels to me, anyway.

say: I'd say five years leaves **no excuse** for firms and government not to plan.
If they **waste the time**, I'd say the blame is theirs, not workers'.
think: At thirty-two I'm young enough to **learn a trade**, but I'd start on apprentice money.
Robots arrive in **2034**, so a hands-on trade only buys a few extra years.
do: Enrol on the town college's **evening plumbing** course, about eight hundred a year.
Keep the **buying job** while studying and save what's left.
Keep pushing the union for **paid training**.
feel: **Scared** but less frozen, seeing a gap he might squeeze through.
S3.quote: A plumbing ticket is mine to keep, wherever I go. An AI course is me training my own replacement for the firm.
fieldNote: He owns the **contradiction**: he'd study a trade on his own time but not AI.
His catalogue knowledge gives him a **head start** in plumbing, and he knows it isn't enough.
Five years turns panic into a **plan**, but money still makes it fragile.

steps.text: Enrol on the town college's evening plumbing course
Keep the buying job while studying and save what's left
Keep pushing the union for firm-paid training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a proper chance and the country should use it. Free training for anyone in a desk job, paid for by the firms that save on wages. I'd post that, and I'd vote for whoever promised it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be thirty-seven. That's enough to finish an apprenticeship, get my plumbing ticket and work a good few years before robots turn up in 2039. I'd still be broke for the first part of it. But it feels like a life I could actually build, not a scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Hollis for now and start the plumbing course in a year or two, once I've got a bit saved. I'd ask Marek, a plumber I know through work, whether he'd take me on as an improver later. And I'd vote and knock on doors for a party that promises paid retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not sick. More like a long list of hard things than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you'd wait to start. What's holding you back from starting now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly, and fear if I'm honest. I don't like jumping when the ground under me still feels solid. With ten years I'd tell myself there's time, and I know that's how people end up doing nothing. Lena would have to nag me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone younger starting as a buyer today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell anyone starting as a buyer not to get comfortable at a desk, and to learn something they can do with their hands. I wish someone had told me that at twenty-two. I spent five years learning a parts catalogue instead.

say: I'd say ten years is a **proper chance** the country should use.
I'd call for **free training** for desk workers, paid by firms that save on wages.
think: At thirty-seven I could have my **plumbing ticket** and years of work before 2039.
The first years would be **broke**, but it feels like a life I could build.
do: Stay at Hollis and start the **plumbing course** in a year or two.
Ask a plumber he knows about an **improver job** later.
Vote and knock on doors for a party promising **paid retraining**.
feel: **Worried** but not sick, like a long list of hard things rather than a cliff.
S4.quote: I'd tell anyone starting as a buyer not to get comfortable at a desk, and to learn something they can do with their hands.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him picture a **trade career**, which calms him a lot.
He admits that time could become an excuse to **do nothing**, and he knows himself.
His politics turn **practical** here: training paid for by the firms that save.

steps.text: Stay on as a buyer at Hollis while saving a little
Start the plumbing course in a year or two
Vote and canvass for a party promising paid retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, no question. Two years is no time when you've got three weeks of rent saved and a job that's all phone and screen. What would help is pay that carries on while you retrain, and a trade course you don't have to pay for up front. And a union that covers office staff, not just the warehouse.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who I blame. People think I'm scared of computers. I'm not, really. I'm scared of a firm that would swap me out and keep every penny it saved. If the savings were shared, I'd feel completely different about all of it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Thank you. That's everything I wanted to ask.

headlineQuote: I'm scared of a firm that would swap me out and keep every penny it saved.
portrait: David is a 27-year-old **plumbing parts buyer** at a regional distributor, renting a small flat with his partner Lena.
He works by **phone and paper**, has never used an AI tool and has about three weeks of rent saved.
He reads every scenario as a **fairness** question about who keeps the savings, and leans on the union.
His mood climbs from uneasy to **panicked** at two years' warning, then eases as the warning time grows.
With five or ten years he'd retrain as a **plumber**, using his parts knowledge as a head start.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his job is all screen and phone and he has almost no savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Pay that continues** while he retrains, and a trade course with no fees up front.
A **union** that covers office staff as well as the warehouse.
